why_angle: ChatGPT's answer put a fridge at 3–5 kWh and used an unsourced 145 W load and an 85% efficiency figure. It gave no measured fridge consumption and did not mention that power stations deliver less at the low loads a fridge draws. This page uses ENERGY STAR's 363 kWh/yr fridge and the roughly 80% low-load yield two reviewers measured on the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2. From those it gives fridge-hours per charge and cost per fridge-day for each station.

page.title: How Much Backup Power Do I Need? Fridge Hours per Power Station (2026)
page.h1: How much backup power do I need?
page.desc: An ENERGY STAR 18 cu ft fridge uses about 1 kWh a day. Measured yields show how many fridge-hours seven power stations give per charge, and what each fridge-day costs.
page.answer: Short answer. For a fridge, the backup power you need is about 1 kWh a day: an ENERGY STAR 18 cu ft model uses 363 kWh/yr (41 W average). A power station delivers about 80% of its rating at that load, so the 2,073.6 Wh BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 runs it about 40 hours.
columns: Fridge hours per charge (41.4 W avg, 80% yield)

cells.capacity: 2,073.6 Wh (APH Networks; BLUETTI's listing says 2,080 Wh)
cells.measured: 2,028 Wh at a 987 W load (APH Networks)
890 Wh (OutdoorGearLab); about 80% at loads in the tens of watts (Techreviewer)

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • The fridge: 363 kWh/yr ÷ 365 = 0.995 kWh a day, and 995 Wh ÷ 24 h = 41.4 W on average. That is ENERGY STAR's figure for an 18 cu ft top-freezer model such as the Crown CRNREF18WT. Other 18–20.5 cu ft top-freezer models on the same list use 362–446 kWh/yr, so redo the sums with your own model's figure.
  • Fridge hours: rated Wh × 0.80 ÷ 41.4 W. For the Elite 200 V2 that is 2,073.6 × 0.80 = 1,659 Wh, and 1,659 ÷ 41.4 = 40.1 h. For the Elite 100 V2 it is 1,024 × 0.80 = 819 Wh, and 819 ÷ 41.4 = 19.8 h. For the Apex 300 it is 2,764.8 × 0.80 = 2,212 Wh, and 2,212 ÷ 41.4 = 53.4 h.
  • Rated size you need: hours × 41.4 W ÷ 0.80. That gives 24 h → 1,242 Wh, 48 h → 2,484 Wh and 72 h → 3,726 Wh.
  • Cost per usable Wh: the Elite 200 V2 costs $899 ÷ 1,659 Wh = $0.54. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 costs $999 ÷ 1,634 Wh = $0.61, and it is on pre-order. The Elite 100 V2 costs $499 ÷ 819 Wh = $0.61.
  • Cost per fridge-day: the Elite 200 V2 costs $899 ÷ 1.67 days = $538. The Elite 100 V2 costs $499 ÷ 0.82 days = $607. The Apex 300 costs $1,499 ÷ 2.22 days = $674, but it is the one that can grow with an add-on battery.

Why a fridge drains a power station faster than its label says

A power station's inverter uses some power just by being switched on, whatever you plug in. At a 500 W load that overhead hardly shows: Techreviewer (Timo Altmeyer) drew 946 Wh from the 1,024 Wh BLUETTI Elite 100 V2. At loads in the tens of watts, the same review found usable capacity fell to about 80%. The Solar Lab also lists 80% efficiency for that unit and calculates a 16 W idle draw. That is about 39% of the 41.4 W an efficient fridge averages, which is why fridge backup gets the low figure. OutdoorGearLab's tests at about 80% of each unit's maximum load put 1 kWh-class stations at 85–87%. That is the moderate-load figure, not the fridge-load one.

The fridge-hours column therefore applies the Elite 100 V2's measured 80% to every station, as a planning figure. Plan on the low-load figure, not the high-load test results: the 98% APH Networks measured at 987 W would overstate the Elite 200 V2's fridge runtime by about 9 hours (2,028 ÷ 41.4 = 49 h, against 40 h).
